claims.claim: An extended literary essay is essentially an argument: the writer argues that a particular interpretation, evaluation, or critical judgment is valid, and the essay needs a specific, debatable thesis statement rather than a statement that merely summarizes the text.

The writing process for a literary essay includes generating ideas, drafting, reviewing, revising, rewriting, and editing; the thesis begins as a working thesis that is subject to revision, because it is nearly impossible to craft a finished thesis before analyzing some of the text.

Quotations must match the source word for word and must be attributed to the original author; paraphrases put a specific passage into your own words and must also be attributed; summaries condense the main ideas of a source into your own words and must be attributed as well.

Direct quotation should be used sparingly and with a good reason; in textual analysis, writers summarize larger ideas in their own language to conserve space, paraphrase more specific ideas, and quote directly to feature the author's diction.

In MLA style, in-text citations use the author-page method: the author's last name and the page number(s) from which the quotation or paraphrase is taken appear in the text, the page number always appears in parentheses, and a complete reference appears on the Works Cited page.

MLA long quotations—more than four typed lines of prose or three lines of verse—are set as a free-standing block indented from the left margin without quotation marks, and the parenthetical citation comes after the closing punctuation.

The Works Cited page is a separate page at the end of the paper: entries are alphabetized by the first element (usually the author's last name), double-spaced with a hanging indent, and every entry must correspond to a source cited in the main text.

Plagiarism is using someone else's ideas or words without giving them proper credit; it ranges from unintentional (forgetting to include a source) to intentional (buying a paper online or passing off another writer's ideas as your own), and it carries serious academic and professional consequences.

Attribution works through three elements used together: a signal phrase naming the source, an in-text citation, and a bibliographic citation such as a Works Cited entry; common knowledge—information documented in at least five credible sources—generally needs no citation, and when in doubt, writers should cite.

Effective revision addresses global feedback first—thesis, topic, and overall organization—before close revision at the sentence level, and body paragraphs support the thesis through topic sentences backed by textual evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Block-quotation indentation has been given different measurements in different handbooks and editions of MLA guidance.
positions: Purdue OWL's current MLA formatting guidance specifies indenting long quotations 1/2 inch from the left margin.
Some instructors and older handbooks expect a one-inch indent for long quotations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the current Purdue OWL figure (1/2 inch) and treats MLA specifics as conventions to confirm against the handbook and instructor requirement for a given course.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Citation styles differ by discipline: MLA uses author-page citations and is standard in U.S. literature courses, while other styles (for example APA) use author-date or other formats.
positions: Purdue OWL's MLA guidance describes the author-page in-text citation method.
Purdue OWL's attribution guidance shows an APA-style citation example with the year, noting that MLA and APA are separate organizations with their own guidelines.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents MLA as the common U.S. academic convention for literary essays while noting that conventions vary by discipline and that the instructor's requirement governs.

conflictingEvidence.issue: 'Common knowledge' has no fixed definition; judgments depend on audience, field, and the availability of documentation.
positions: Purdue OWL defines common knowledge as information undocumented in at least five credible sources.
Instructors and disciplines may apply the label differently depending on the audience and assignment.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the practical rule: common knowledge generally needs no citation, and when in doubt, cite.
